actual_context.text:
<Tip>

This page only contains information on the `st.cache_data` API. For a deeper dive into caching and how to use it, check out [Caching](/develop/concepts/architecture/caching).

</Tip>

<Autofunction function="streamlit.cache_data" oldName="streamlit.experimental_memo" />

<Warning>

`st.cache_data` implicitly uses the `pickle` module, which is known to be insecure. Anything your cached function returns is pickled and stored, then unpickled on retrieval. Ensure your cached functions return trusted values because it is possible to construct malicious pickle data that will execute arbitrary code during unpickling. Never load data that could have come from an untrusted source in an unsafe mode or that could have been tampered with. **Only load data you trust**.

</Warning>

<Autofunction function="streamlit.cache_data.clear" oldName="streamlit.experimental_memo.clear" />

parent.title: caching
parent.text:
#### Behavior
How does this work? Let's go through the behavior of `st.cache_data` step by step: - On the first run, Streamlit recognizes that it has never called the `load_data` function with the specified parameter value (the URL of the CSV file) So it runs the function and downloads the data. - Now our caching mechanism becomes active: the returned DataFrame is serialized (converted to bytes) via [pickle](https://docs.python.org/3/library/pickle.html) and stored in the cache (together with the value of the `url` parameter). - On the next run, Streamlit checks the cache for an entry of `load_data` with the specific `url`. There is one! So it retrieves the cached object, deserializes it to a DataFrame, and returns it instead of re-running the function and downloading the data again. This process of serializing and deserializing the cached object creates a copy of our original DataFrame. While this copying behavior may seem unnecessary, it's what we want when caching data objects since it effectively prevents mutation and concurrency issues. Read the section “[Mutation and concurrency issues](#mutation-and-concurrency-issues)" below to understand this in more detail. `st.cache_data` implicitly uses the `pickle` module, which is known to be insecure. Anything your cached function returns is pickled and stored, then unpickled on retrieval. Ensure your cached functions return trusted values because it is possible to construct malicious pickle data that will execute arbitrary code during unpickling. Never load data that could have come from an untrusted source in an unsafe mode or that could have been tampered with. **Only load data you trust**.

This process of serializing and deserializing the cached object creates a copy of our original DataFrame. While this copying behavior may seem unnecessary, it's what we want when caching data objects since it effectively prevents mutation and concurrency issues. Read the section “[Mutation and concurrency issues](#mutation-and-concurrency-issues)" below to understand this in more detail. `st.cache_data` implicitly uses the `pickle` module, which is known to be insecure. Anything your cached function returns is pickled and stored, then unpickled on retrieval. Ensure your cached functions return trusted values because it is possible to construct malicious pickle data that will execute arbitrary code during unpickling. Never load data that could have come from an untrusted source in an unsafe mode or that could have been tampered with. **Only load data you trust**.

Streamlit does not know how to hash custom classes. If you pass a custom class to a cached function, Streamlit will raise a `UnhashableParamError`. multiplier = 2


```python

```


To fix this, we can use the `hash_funcs` parameter to tell Streamlit how to hash `MyCustomClass`. We do this by passing a dictionary to `hash_funcs` that maps the name of the parameter to a hash function. The choice of hash function is up to the developer. In this case, let's define a custom hash function `hash_func` that takes the custom class as input and returns the score. We want the score to be the unique identifier of the object, so we can use it to deterministically hash the object:

```python
import streamlit as st

class MyCustomClass:
    def __init__(self, initial_score: int):
        self.my_score = initial_score

def hash_func(obj: MyCustomClass) -> int:
    return obj.my_score  # or any other value that uniquely identifies the object

@st.cache_data(hash_funcs={MyCustomClass: hash_func})
def multiply_score(obj: MyCustomClass, multiplier: int) -> int:
    return obj.my_score * multiplier

initial_score = st.number_input("Enter initial score", value=15)

score = MyCustomClass(initial_score)
multiplier = 2

st.write(multiply_score(score, multiplier))
```

Now if you run the app, you'll see that Streamlit no longer raises a `UnhashableParamError` and the app runs as expected.

Let's now consider the case where `multiply_score` is an attribute of `MyCustomClass` and we want to hash the entire object:

```python

class MyCustomClass:
    def __init__(self, initial_score: int):
        self.my_score = initial_score

    @st.cache_data

        return self.my_score * multiplier

multiplier = 2

st.write(score.multiply_score(multiplier))
```

initial_candidates.title: cache-data
initial_candidates.text:
### Static elements

Since version 1.16.0, cached functions can contain Streamlit commands! For example, you can do this:

```python
@st.cache_data
def get_api_data():
    data = api.get(...)
    st.success("Fetched data from API!")  # 👈 Show a success message
    return data
```

As we know, Streamlit only runs this function if it hasn’t been cached before. On this first run, the `st.success` message will appear in the app. But what happens on subsequent runs? It still shows up! Streamlit realizes that there is an `st.` command inside the cached function, saves it during the first run, and replays it on subsequent runs. Replaying static elements works for both caching decorators.

You can also use this functionality to cache entire parts of your UI:

```python
@st.cache_data
def show_data():
    st.header("Data analysis")
    data = api.get(...)
    st.success("Fetched data from API!")
    st.write("Here is a plot of the data:")
    st.line_chart(data)
    st.write("And here is the raw data:")
    st.dataframe(data)
```

initial_candidates.title: download_button with data=callable runs without ScriptRunContext
initial_candidates.text:
### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.52.2
- Python version: 3.13
- Operating System: Win
- Browser: Chrome

Somehow I missed this issue https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/13337
Closing as duplicate

Confirming this from a production incident — and it's a bit worse than "missing ScriptRunContext produces a warning": inside that thread, `st.session_state` reads return stale values and `@st.cache_data`-wrapped calls silently return whatever was already cached, **with no error and no warning**. Both just look like they worked.

Our incident: a `data=callable` on `st.download_button` called into functions that (transitively) read `@st.cache_data`-cached helpers. Because those calls run outside `ScriptRunContext`, they picked up cached results from a *different* request context — users occasionally downloaded a file that didn't match what they'd just generated on screen, with nothing in the logs to explain why. We only found the mechanism by tracing the full call graph of the callable, not just inspecting it — a lambda that looks pure can still be unsafe if anything it calls touches cached/session state indirectly.

### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.52.2
- Python version: 3.13
- Operating System: Win
- Browser: Chrome

Somehow I missed this issue https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/13337
Closing as duplicate

Confirming this from a production incident — and it's a bit worse than "missing ScriptRunContext produces a warning": inside that thread, `st.session_state` reads return stale values and `@st.cache_data`-wrapped calls silently return whatever was already cached, **with no error and no warning**. Both just look like they worked.

Our incident: a `data=callable` on `st.download_button` called into functions that (transitively) read `@st.cache_data`-cached helpers. Because those calls run outside `ScriptRunContext`, they picked up cached results from a *different* request context — users occasionally downloaded a file that didn't match what they'd just generated on screen, with nothing in the logs to explain why. We only found the mechanism by tracing the full call graph of the callable, not just inspecting it — a lambda that looks pure can still be unsafe if anything it calls touches cached/session state indirectly.

We ended up moving off lazy `data=` entirely (eager bytes, pre-warmed at save time) because we couldn't make the callable's dependency tree provably free of session/cache reads. For anyone hitting this: if your callable calls anything that isn't a pure function of its arguments, the missing context isn't just a perf/warning issue, it's a correctness one.

initial_candidates.title: Deduplicate identical `st.cache_data` return values to save memory
initial_candidates.text:
### Summary

`st.cache_data` stores one serialized (pickled) blob per cache key, where the key is derived only from the function + input arguments. If a function returns the *same* value (e.g. the same dataframe) for many different inputs, each of those cache entries stores a full, redundant copy. We could recognize identical serialized return values (e.g. by hashing the serialized value bytes) and store the payload only once, with each cache key referencing it — saving memory (and disk when persisted).
